translations.text: Judas, also called Maccabeus, and others with him, numbering ten, withdrew into the mountains. They lived like wild animals, eating grass and keeping apart so that they would not share in the defilement.
After a short time, the king sent an elderly Athenian to force the Jews to abandon their ancestors’ laws and no longer live according to them,
and to defile the temple in Jerusalem, calling it the temple of Olympian Zeus, and the one in Chorazin, calling it the temple of Zeus the Protector of Strangers, according to the request
of those who lived there. The evil that had come upon them was exceedingly great and hard for everyone to bear.
For the temple was filled with debauchery and revelry by the Gentiles. They committed indecent acts with women who lay in the sacred porticoes, and they brought inappropriate things inside.
They placed defiled things on the altar, things that the law had forbidden.
For there was no possibility of keeping the Sabbath or observing our ancestors’ festivals, or even acknowledging that they were Jews.

Every month, on the king’s birthday, they were brought under harsh compulsion to offer sacrifices. When the festival of Dionysus arrived, they were forced to walk in procession before him with wreaths on their heads.
Ptolemy sent an order to the neighboring Greek cities to treat the Jews in the same way and make them offer sacrifices.
Those who would not agree to adopt Greek customs were to be killed.
The other evil they committed was also severe. Two women had circumcised their little children [?] their breasts. They paraded them throughout the whole city and threw them down.

Others fled secretly into nearby tombs so as not to celebrate the Sabbath. Philip was informed about them, and he threw them out, because they were afraid to defend themselves out of respect for that honored, sacred day.
I therefore beg those who read this book not to lose heart over these sufferings, but to consider that these afflictions happen to our people not to destroy them, but to discipline them.
For not allowing us to go astray, but punishing them immediately, is a great sign of goodness.
For the Lord did not judge us as he does the Gentiles, toward whom he remains patient until they reach the full measure, and then punishes them,
lest we too reach the full measure of our sins and he take vengeance on us.
For this reason, he has not removed his mercy from us forever. Rather, while disciplining his people through afflictions, he does not abandon us.
But we have mentioned these things as a reminder. Now let us speak briefly about what happened.
Eleazar was one of the leading scribes, a man advanced in age, dignified and handsome in appearance. They forced him to eat pork.
But he sought an honorable death for himself rather than a life of shame, and willingly gave himself over to torture.
He spat it out, as is fitting for those who wish to stand firm [?] life.

Those appointed to oversee the unlawful sacrifice, because of their longstanding friendship with the man, took him aside and urged him to let them bring him meat he had prepared himself, of the kind they ate. He was to pretend to eat from the sacrifices the king had ordered, so that by this means
they might spare him from death.

But he considered the matter with sound judgment, worthy of his honored old age, his blameless way of life, his good conduct from childhood, and the holy law established by God. He answered, saying, “Send me to the underworld at once.
It is not fitting at my age to pretend, lest many young children think that Eleazar, at ninety years old, has turned to a Gentile way of life,
and they be led astray by his pretense, while through this little, miserable life I bring defilement and shame upon myself in my old age.
Even if I escape human swords now, I will not escape the hand of the Almighty, whether I live or die.”
Therefore I will now die courageously and show myself worthy of my old age.

And I will leave the young people an example of courage, so that they too may die eagerly and resolutely for the holy law and stand firm.” As soon as he said these things, he went forward to the torture.
Those who had been distressed over him afterward became angry with him because of what he had said, saying, “What recklessness!”

When he was about to die, he groaned and said, “It is clear to the Lord, who knows everything, that I could have been released from death. I endure severe pains in my body as they whip me, but in my soul I welcome these sufferings because I fear him.”
Thus he fell asleep, leaving his death as an example of courage and a memorial of virtue, not only for the young people but also for most of his nation.
It also happened that seven other brothers and their mother were being forced by the king to eat from the unclean sacrifice, while they were beaten with whips and cords.
One of them was the first to speak, saying, “What are you questioning us about, or what will you hear from us? For we are ready to die rather than violate the laws of our ancestors.”
The king became angry and ordered fires to be lit under pans and bronze pots.

When they were hot, he ordered the tongue of the one who had spoken first to be cut out, his skin to be stripped off, and his bones to be [?] out, while his brothers and his mother watched him. When he had been completely mutilated,
while he was still breathing, he ordered him to be lifted up into the [?] pan. As the smoke from the pan rose more and more, they and their mother urged one another on, saying:
Let us too die courageously, for the Lord God fights for us, as Moses said in his song that bears witness: “Compassion will be shown to his servants.”

After the first had died in this way, they brought the second, mocking him. They stripped the skin from his head along with his hair and asked him, “Will you eat before your body is tortured limb by limb?”
But he answered in the language of his ancestors, saying, “Just as the first endured the torture, so will I.”
When he was about to give up his spirit, he said, “You, evildoer, will release us from this life, but the King of the world will raise us to live forever, because we have died for his laws.”
After this, they brought in the third and demanded his tongue. He immediately put it out and raised his hands.
He was resolute, saying courageously, “These were given to me from heaven, and I disregard them because I fear him and honor his law, believing that I will receive them again from him.”
The king and those with him were amazed at the young man’s spirit, at how he considered suffering to be nothing.
When this one had died, they tortured the fourth in the same way, beating him.
When he was about to die, he said, “It is better for us to die at human hands while looking forward with hope to God raising us again. But for you there will be no resurrection to life.”
They also brought the fifth in the same way and tortured him. He looked into the king’s face and said:
“You are a human being who will perish, yet you have received authority over people and do whatever you want. So do not think that God has abandoned our people.
Just watch how he will torture you and your descendants.”
After this they brought the sixth. When he was about to die, he said, “Do not be foolishly deceived, for we are suffering these things because of the sins we have committed against our God.
But do not think that you will escape while fighting against God.”
Their mother was especially remarkable and worthy of being remembered with honor. She watched seven sons perish together in a single day and endured it courageously because of her hope in God.
She encouraged each of them in her own language, filled with courage, stirring her womanly mind with a man’s anger, and saying to them:
“I do not know how you came to be within me. Nor was it I who gave you life, breath, or the body of each of you.”
“Now the Creator of the whole world, who formed humanity and all other things, has also given you the breath of life in his mercy, since you have disregarded yourselves for the sake of his law.”

Antiochus, however, said, “They are treating me with contempt.” Noticing the tone meant to mock him, and while the youngest of them was still alive, he pleaded with him, not only with words but also with oaths, trying to persuade him: “I will make you rich and happy if you turn away from the laws of your ancestors. I will make you my friend and give you positions of authority.”
When the young boy paid no attention, the king called his mother and begged her to persuade the young boy to save his life.
When she heard this, she bowed down at the young boy’s feet.

Mocking the [?] tyrant, she spoke to him this way in her own language: “My son, have pity on me, who carried you in the womb for nine months and nursed you for three years. I raised you and brought you to this size.
I beg you, my son, to look at heaven and earth and everything in them, and to understand that God made them out of things that did not exist. The human race also came into being in this way.
Do not be afraid of the murderer. Instead, prove yourself worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that in God’s dwelling he may give you back to me along with your brothers.”

Before she had finished these words, the young boy said, “Who are you waiting for? I will not obey the king’s command. Instead, I will obey the command of the law of Moses, which he gave to our ancestors.
But you, who plot every kind of evil against the Hebrews, will not escape God’s hand.
For we have suffered these things because of our sins, as our living Lord disciplines us.
He has been angry with us for a short time to teach us, but afterward he will be reconciled with his servants. You have not yet escaped the judgment of God Almighty.
But you, unclean one, enemy of everyone, do not be vainly arrogant, relying on empty hopes, when you have risen up against the children of heaven.
For my brothers, after enduring a little suffering, have now entered into God’s covenant. But you will receive, under his judgment, a punishment worthy of your arrogance.

I too, like my other brothers, will give my body and my soul for the laws of my ancestors, calling on God to forgive our people quickly and, through afflictions and scourges, to make you acknowledge that he alone is God.
And may the wrath of the Almighty, which he justly brought upon our whole people, come to an end with me and my brothers.”
The king became angrier with this one than with all the others. He killed him himself, feeling ashamed at the way the young man had mocked him.
This is how this one too died in purity, trusting in the Lord until the end.
After all the sons, their mother also died.
